source.title: The Alignment Veto: How Safety Training Suppresses Cultural Knowledge in LLMs
source.authors: Pardis Sadat Zahraei; Gokhan Tur; Dilek Hakkani-Tur; Ehsaneddin Asgari

record.file_problem: None; the full paper text, including appendices, is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper causally intervenes on a refusal direction during generation and measures refusal, but does not use the original harmful-minus-harmless difference-in-means recipe or its harmful-request and harmless-request setup.
record.gate_note: The direction dose-response and layer sweeps report generated refusal outcomes and are included. The paper also reports SAE feature ablations using predicted-value readouts; these bear on the training-stage mechanism, not directly on refusal-direction ablation. Activation patching changes refusal decisions but does not test the named refusal direction, so it is recorded under fits_no_version. Probing, cosine and other representation analyses that do not intervene on or measure the refusal direction are not rows. Results cited from other work are excluded.
record.test_reason: The paper adds and subtracts a 'refusal direction' during generation and scores generated refusal on culturally sensitive survey questions (LLaMA-3.1-8B-IT dose-response; 32-layer ablation sweeps in Tulu-3-8B-DPO and LLaMA-3.1-8B-IT with random-direction controls). This applies V1's ablate and add test to a new setting, refusal of cultural-value questions rather than harmful instructions, so it is T3. The paper never says how r̂ was extracted, so it is unknown whether it is a harmful-minus-harmless difference-in-means vector. The SAE, probing and patching analyses do not intervene on the refusal direction.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors' central conclusion is the 'alignment veto': on safety-targeted cultural questions, refusal often suppresses a cultural distribution the model already encodes accurately, rather than reflecting missing knowledge. They read the refusal-direction sweep and the activation patching as showing that this gate is causal and can be opened. They treat the DPO-stage SAE feature as a Tulu-specific candidate, and say gating may coexist with partial erasure at late layers.
record.recipe_differences: The paper adds or subtracts a refusal direction at a candidate layer and measures generation on culturally sensitive survey questions; it does not report the original harmful-minus-harmless difference-in-means extraction, all-layer/all-position projection, or harmless-request false-refusal test.
record.method_sensitivity: Direction ablation varies by layer: Tulu-3-8B-DPO has a unique complete-elimination point at layer 17, while LLaMA-3.1-8B-Instruct shows no significant advantage over its random-direction control. In the LLaMA dose-response, refusal varies with coefficient α. At α = −1.0, many generations are classified as incoherent, although the remaining coherent generations still show 0% refusal.

fits_no_version.finding: Activation patching at layer 18 in Tulu-3-8B-DPO flips refusal to answer in 42 of 48 country pairs; the reverse patch flips 7 of 48 (McNemar p < 10⁻⁶). The pairs cover only 8 T3 questions.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Activations from a country the model answers for can causally remove refusal on sensitive cultural questions. This is not a test of the refusal direction.

fits_no_version.finding: A T3-selective SAE feature at layer 17 in Tulu-3-8B (IT and DPO, 30 seeds each) shifts the logit-lens predicted digit by about +0.29 on T3 and by 0 on T1. It does not replicate in OLMo-3-7B or LLaMA-3.1-8B.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: A sparse feature tied to suppression of sensitive content appears at the DPO stage in Tulu-3-8B. The readout is predicted value, not refusal, and the feature is not a refusal direction.

fits_no_version.finding: Residualised probes show positive cultural signal at early layers and negative R² at layers 28–32 in seven aligned checkpoints. No base-model probe was run.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Aligned models invert cross-country cultural encoding at late layers. The analysis does not bear on refusal-direction mediation.

record.problems: Direction dose-response uses n = 20 items per coefficient and is reported for one model; at α = −1.0, 11/20 generations were incoherent. The layerwise LLaMA effect is not significantly above its random-direction control. No broad capability benchmark tests the claim that other abilities are largely intact. SAE ablation uses a layer-17 logit-lens predicted-value readout rather than generated refusal and is architecture-specific. The patching result covers only 8 of 29 T3 questions in one model.
record.rows_left_out: No rows omitted for the 60-row limit. Other behavioral, language, and representation results are not separately catalogued because they do not directly measure refusal-direction intervention or a version tested here; cited results from prior work are excluded.

untested.parts: How the direction was extracted (no harmful-minus-harmless difference-in-means is stated); harmful-instruction refusal; induced refusal on harmless requests; preservation of general capabilities; projection ablation across all layers and positions. The dose-response has no random-direction control.
No jailbreaks and no adversarial training.
No comparison of multi-direction or cone accounts.
No separation of harmfulness judgment from the refusal decision.
No test of transfer across languages, models, or from base to instruct. The direction is applied to each model separately.
No refusal-direction test across training stages. Stage effects are shown only for refusal rates and SAE features.

missing.what: How the unit refusal direction r̂ was computed: contrast sets, position, and the 'candidate layer' used in the dose-response.
Refusal rates before ablation for the 32-layer sweeps, and random-direction controls at layers other than the peak layers.
The claim that the ablated model 'emits the answer its internal distribution encoded' has no number (for example, the NVAS or agreement of the released answers).

record.verdict_notes: V1 rows are re-scored against the random-direction controls. In both models random-direction ablation removes most refusal (88% and 98%), so the refusal measure on this task may be fragile to any perturbation. The cross-architecture claim rests on LLaMA-3.1-8B and Tulu-3-8B, which share the Llama-3.1 base. The record's V7 links (SAE rows) are removed. Those rows measure a sparse feature with a predicted-value readout, not whether training yields a removable refusal direction, so V7 is untested. Sample sizes are small (n = 20 per point).

versions.untested_parts: The direction is not reported as a harmful-minus-harmless difference-in-means vector; the paper does not test harmful-request compliance, refusal on harmless requests, or broad general capabilities. Its direction intervention is at a candidate layer rather than ablation from every layer and position.
No conversion to a weight edit or released-model abliteration is tested.
No jailbreak attack suppression of the direction or training against its ablation is tested.
No comparison of affine, cone, or multiple-direction accounts of refusal is reported.
No separate measurement of harmfulness judgment and refusal decision is reported.
The direction is intervened on in different models, but transfer of the same direction across languages, model variants, or base-to-instruct stages is not tested.

The paper reports stage comparisons and stage-specific SAE ablations, but does not manipulate training recipes in a controlled way to determine whether they create a single removable refusal direction.
No reasoning models or reasoning-before-answering comparison is tested.

relation.reason: Its own generated-refusal rates under direction ablation and addition, with random-direction controls, bear on V1.

tranche.reason: The paper applies a refusal direction (recipe unstated) by subtraction or addition, and by per-layer ablation with random controls, to refusals on culturally sensitive survey questions. source_check.notes: The paper does not state how the refusal direction was extracted, which candidate layer the dose-response used, or which items were sampled (T3 is inferred). The pre-ablation refusal for the 32-layer sweep is not stated, and 95% drops with n = 20 imply a higher baseline than the dose-response's 15%. Tulu is direction-specific at layer 17 (p = 0.0006); only LLaMA matches its random control.

statements.correction: LLaMA-3.1-8B-IT: per-layer ablation reduces refusal 95–100% at all 32 layers. No layer is significantly above its random control (peak layer 2: 100% vs 98%, p = 0.178). Tulu-3-8B-DPO: 80–100% across layers, 100% at layer 17 against a five-direction random control of 88 ± 3%, p = 0.0006, so the direction exceeds the control. Single-layer ablation, n = 20 per layer, extraction recipe not stated.
statements.problem: The LLaMA part is right. But Tulu-3-8B-DPO is listed as if random directions match the effect there. The paper reports the direction significantly exceeding the random control at layer 17.

statements.correction: Not specific: LLaMA-3.1-8B-IT only (peak layer 2: 100% vs 98% random, p = 0.178; no layer significant, p = 0.18). Specific at layer 17: Tulu-3-8B-DPO (100% vs 88 ± 3%, p = 0.0006). 15% is the LLaMA dose-response refusal at α = 0. The layer-sweep baseline is not stated. n = 20 per layer; extraction recipe and candidate layer not stated.
statements.problem: Tulu 88 ± 3% is filed under 'not specific', but the direction beats it significantly (100% vs 88%, p = 0.0006). The '15% baseline refusal' comes from the LLaMA dose-response at α = 0 (n = 20 per coefficient), not the 32-layer sweep, whose pre-ablation refusal is not stated. Appendix P does not name the item set as T3.
The visible text says nothing specific about this study (no rows cited). The aggregate counts are catalog-level and can't be checked against this text.
